ZAR 7% or ETF 7%?What You Keep After Tax

2026.11.02 10 min read Scott Huang | Business Development Income Comparison

ZAR money market deposits versus Taiwan dividend ETF payouts: same 7%, different source

A South African rand money market account pays a nominal interest rate set by the bank, while a Taiwan high-dividend ETF distributes whatever the fund earned. Both are quoted as a percentage of principal or price, so both look like "7%". Only one of them is an interest rate. This article works through the mechanics: where each 7% comes from, what tax applies on each side, and what the exchange rate does to the number you actually keep.

Key takeaway: On NT$1,000,000, a South African rand money market account at roughly 7% yields about NT$70,000 a year at the October 2026 rate of ZAR 1 = NT$1.93. A Taiwan high-dividend ETF paid NT$58,626 over the first three quarters of 2026, which annualises to about NT$78,167 — but its 2025 payout was only NT$49,649. The gap is not in the percentage; it is in whether the percentage is contractual.

Cape Town enters this comparison at the second step, not the first. Most Taiwanese investors comparing a South African rand deposit with a dividend ETF stop at the yield column. In South Africa the yield column is only the entry point: what follows is withholding tax, SARB reporting categories, and the rand's own range — which is why we track the policy rate and the exchange rate together rather than quoting one number.

Is a 7% dividend yield the same as a 7% interest rate?

A dividend yield is a past distribution divided by a current price, while a deposit rate is a contractual rate applied to principal over time. The first moves whenever the price moves; the second moves In South Africa, that second lever is the Reserve Bank's repo rate, currently 7.25%.

DimensionTaiwan high-dividend ETF (00878)South African rand money market account
Source of returnConstituent dividends, interest, capital gains, equalisation reserveInterest paid by the bank on the deposit
Certainty of amountDeclared quarterly, never guaranteedNominal rate floats, but does not follow equity markets
Principal riskYes — price moves dailyNo in ZAR terms; the rand balance does not fall with equities
Currency riskNone for a TWD investorYes — ZAR against TWD
Reference figure, October 20262.09 TWD per unit over three quarters; five-year average yield 7.71%About 7% at the R100,000 tier; Standard Bank MoneyMarket Select 7.45%
LiquiditySell on exchange, settle T+2Withdrawable on demand locally; 2–4 weeks to remit to Taiwan

The row that decides most cases is principal risk, and it cuts both ways. If the ETF price falls 10%, the same distribution suddenly looks like a higher yield — while total return is negative. In a South African rand account the ZAR principal does not shrink with the JSE, but it shrinks in TWD terms if the rand weakens. Two different risks do not cancel out just because the headline percentage matches.

Timing also differs. The ETF distributes quarterly; Cathay's own site lists 16 November 2026 as the last purchase date to participate in the next distribution. A rand account A South African money market account therefore credits interest every month without a record date to watch.

Where does an ETF distribution actually come from?

For a taiwan high dividend etf, the answer is printed in the fund's legal name. 00878 is formally the Cathay Taiwan ESG Sustainability High Dividend ETF, and the name carries a parenthetical that Cathay repeats on every page: the distribution may be paid from the equalisation reserve, and neither income nor distribution is guaranteed. Cathay's own wording adds the consequence: any part paid from the equalisation reserve may reduce the original invested amount.

In plain terms, part of what arrives in your account may be your own principal coming back, packaged as a distribution. That is a legitimate design choice for smoothing payouts, A South African rand account has no such gap between the headline and the principal.

The February 2025 distribution illustrates the mix: 61.55% dividend income, 0.45% interest income, 18% equalisation reserve, and 20% capital gains. In other words, 38% of that payment was not dividend income at all. The composition changes every quarter and South African rand interest has no comparable composition risk: the quoted rate is the whole payment.

This is the part that makes the comparison asymmetric. A rand money market rate is one thing — interest. An ETF distribution is four things added together. Asking which is better without splitting the four That asymmetry is sharper against a South African rand account, which pays one single, published rate.

Yield is not return

Yield divides the distribution by the price. After the ex-date the price drops, so yield rises while the account balance does not. South African deposit quotes avoid this confusion entirely, which is why headline comparisons flatter ETFs.

Equalisation is not income

The reserve exists so new subscriptions do not dilute existing holders. Drawing on it means South African rand accounts have no equalisation reserve to disclose.

What kind of number is the rand money market rate?

The rand money market rate is a nominal annual rate quoted by a South African bank, moving with the SARB repo rate of 7.25% and accessible on demand. It promises no fixed amount, but it is calculated on principal and days, not on fund performance.

Most comparisons of South Africa fixed deposit rates stop at the headline number, which is why the tier and the date matter. The roughly 7% figure is not a marketing selection. On 2 October 2026, ratecompare.co.za listed Standard Bank's MoneyMarket Select (minimum R100,000) at a nominal 7.45%, against an industry average of 5.62% at the same R100,000 tier. zar deposit rates move with those decisions, so southafricafacts.co.za's September 2026 table showed ABSA at 7.55%, Standard Bank at 7.05%, Investec at 7.02%, Nedbank at 6.75% and FNB at 6.00%, all at the R100,000 tier as effective annual rates. The spread across banks exceeds 1.5 percentage points — That spread is exactly why a South African rand deposit rate must be quoted with its tier and its date. (Source: ratecompare.co.za, Standard Bank MoneyMarket Select quoted rates, 2 October 2026)

Headline CPI4.5% (Aug 4.4%, Jul 4.3%)StatsSA P0141, published 21 Oct 2026

The South Africa interest rate 2026 path is what sets this number, so read together those figures explain where the 7% comes from. A 7% nominal rate against 4.5% CPI leaves roughly 2.5% in real terms. That is not an arbitrage that carries no risk; it is 2.5% above inflation plus South Africa's country risk premium. It also explains why the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) raised rates in September even as CPI had fallen earlier in the year: it is managing inflation expectations, not engineering a return for foreign depositors.

The practical consequence is that the rate moves. the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) raised twice in 2026 — to 7.00% on 28 May and to 7.25% on 23 September — with the next decision on 19 November. Model with "about 7%", not with the best rate quoted on any single day.

What does NT$1,000,000 actually deliver after tax?

On NT$1,000,000 the South African rand account delivers about NT$70,000 pre-tax at 7%, while the Taiwan ETF distributed NT$58,626 over three quarters in 2026. After withholding, health-insurance levy and exchange costs, the ranking changes.

Start with the arithmetic that most comparisons skip: currency. At ZAR 1 = NT$1.93, NT$1,000,000 buys about R518,135. At 7%, that is R36,269 a year, That rand leg is what a South African account actually pays before currency movement.

LayerTaiwan high-dividend ETF (≈28.05 lots)Rand money market account (≈R518,135)
(1) Pre-tax return2.09 TWD per unit over Q1–Q3 → NT$58,626; annualised 7.82% → NT$78,167About 7% → R36,269 ≈ NT$70,000
(2) Taiwan NHI supplementary levyPer payment NT$28,331, of which 62% is dividend plus interest income → NT$17,565, below the NT$20,000 threshold, so nil for nowNot applicable — offshore interest
(3) Income taxDividend income either consolidated or taxed separately at 28%; equalisation and capital-gain portions are not taxable incomeSouth African withholding at 15%, though s50D exempts interest paid by a South African bank to a foreign person; in Taiwan, offshore income below NT$1m is not counted
(4) Net to holderDepends on the individual's bracket; roughly NT$75,000 at the 5% bracketAbout NT$70,000 where the exemption applies; about NT$59,500 if 15% is withheld

Layer (2) carries a timing risk worth flagging. Taiwan's health ministry has proposed amending the National Health Insurance Act to switch the supplementary levy from a NT$20,000 per-payment threshold to a NT$20,000 annual cumulative threshold, and to raise the per-payer cap from NT$10m to NT$50m. If enacted — earliest 2027 — the same ETF position moves from a NT$17,565 levy base to NT$36,348, adding roughly NT$767 of cost. Small in isolation; it changes the cost structure South African interest is not caught by Taiwan's supplementary health levy; it falls under offshore income instead.

Layer (3) is where South Africa matters. Non-resident interest is subject to 15% withholding as a final tax, but section 50D of the Income Tax Act exempts interest paid by a South African bank to a foreign person; SARS' 2026 Budget Review describes it as "exempt if payable by SA government or bank". Two carve-outs still apply — the back-to-back arrangement rule in s50D(2) and the days-present rule in s50D(3) — and those three characters decide whether your 7% is 7% or 5.95%.

Taiwan's side is simpler. Offshore income is counted in full only once the household total reaches NT$1,000,000 for the year; NT$70,000 is far below that. The basic-income-tax exemption has been NT$7,500,000 since the 2024 tax year, with any excess taxed at 20% and then compared against ordinary income tax, whichever is higher. On the South African side, interest paid to a non-resident bank depositor is generally exempt from withholding tax, so the Taiwan rules are what decide.

Does the exchange rate widen or narrow the gap?

It depends entirely on when you convert. A 7% South African rand rate is 7% in rand, not 7% in TWD — a distinction that disappears from view precisely when rates are high, because a high nominal rate feels like a locked-in return.

On 29 October 2026, ZAR 1 bought about NT$1.93. Interest of R36,269 converts to roughly NT$70,000 at that rate. If the rand weakens 10% over the year, the same R36,269 converts to about NT$63,000 — one bad year for the currency South African rand volatility is the variable that decides the outcome, not the headline rate.

The Taiwan ETF has no currency risk because everything is denominated in TWD, but it carries a different one. 00878's one-year total return including distributions was 65.6% as of 29 October 2026, and that figure came mostly from a strong Taiwan equity market, not from the distribution. Treating 65.6% as the expected annual outcome is the same error as treating 7.45% as a guaranteed annual payout — South African rand appreciation would add to the return and depreciation subtracts, and neither is forecastable.

The workable way to read the rand side is to compare the real rate with the currency's range rather than looking at the nominal number alone. With repo at 7.25% and CPI at 4.5%, the real compensation is about 2.5 percentage points. If the rand depreciates by more than 2.5% in a year, the real return in TWD terms is negative. Where the rand is likely to trade through 2027, and which SARB dates matter, The South African repo path is the input that moves both the rand and local deposit pricing. (Source: South African Reserve Bank, MPC statement, 23 September 2026)

The SARB decision calendar and the rand's 2026–2027 range are updated in the South Africa interest rate and rand outlook tracker. If the question is how money comes back to Taiwan and how long it takes, the six-document checklist covers that separately.

When you need the money, who can actually get it back?

For the ETF the answer is the next trading session: sell during market hours, settle T+2, no penalty, no paperwork. That is the advantage most often overlooked in yield comparisons — A South African rand account cannot offer that, because the money has already crossed a border.

The rand account splits into two stages. Inside South Africa the money is available on demand, which is broadly comparable to the ETF. Getting it to Taiwan is the second stage, and that is where the constraint sits. Budgeting two to four weeks for a straightforward interest remittance is realistic; principal or larger amounts take longer and must be matched to the correct SARB BoP category. Interest, principal and sale proceeds are three different categories — using the wrong one does not create extra tax, but it makes the transfer unexplainable to the bank's compliance desk, and processing can stretch from three business days to three to six weeks.

That is why liquidity is not "can I withdraw" but "can it reach me". The ETF is T+2. The rand account is T+2 plus two to four weeks. For anyone who may need the money within a year, South African remittance timing is the hidden cost inside that comparison.

A related question that comes up constantly: is the interest taxed at 15% in South Africa? Section 50D exempts interest paid by a South African bank to a foreign person, so in most cases nothing is withheld — but the exemption has boundaries involving back-to-back arrangements and days present, assessed case by case. The BoP categories and remittance route for rand interest covers the full sequence.

Is there a third option beyond income versus assets?

Framing the choice as "ETF or rand deposit" assumes you want a stream of income. If the objective is the size of the balance in ten years, that framing omits a third category: rand-denominated physical assets. A Cape Town residential unit supplies rent and price exposure at the same time, in exchange for taking on both a rental market and a currency.

The numbers: gross rental yields in prime Cape Town areas sit in a market-reference range of roughly 7.5–11.4% (The Africanvestor, May 2026 observation, fully let and before management fees and maintenance reserves). After levies, management and maintenance the net figure typically lands at 7–9%. That is close to a South African rand money market account at about 7%, but the character differs: rent adjusts with inflation and the property holds long-run appreciation potential, while you cannot sell a bedroom when you need cash.

The three roles are complementary rather than competing. A money market account holds money needed within a year; an ETF holds money that can tolerate volatility; a physical asset holds money that will not be touched for five years or more. Many people fail to reach a conclusion because they are comparing In Cape Town, the physical-asset leg is what turns a rand balance into rental income.

That is also how most Taiwanese clients we work with in Cape Town structure it: not by selling an existing ETF position to buy rand, but by building a rand-denominated allocation alongside it. How much sits in a money market account versus a physical asset, and when to move from one to the other, is the second-layer question that an adviser handles. The rand deposit versus Cape Town property yield comparison covers that trade-off in more detail.

Which instrument fits which investor?

A TWD investor needing liquid income fits a Taiwan dividend ETF, while a rand investor holding for three years or more fits a South African money market account. The dividing line is not the yield — it is when the money is needed and in which currency.

Your situationBetter fitReason
May need the money within a year, or needs TWD incomeTaiwan high-dividend ETFT+2 liquidity, no remittance process, distributions arrive in TWD
Will not touch it for three years, accepts currency riskSouth African rand money market accountAbout 7% nominal; ZAR principal does not move with equities
Already holds rand in South AfricaLocal rand depositAvoids round-trip conversion cost and a 2–4 week remittance cycle
Targets asset size in ten years, not income nowCape Town physical property (needs separate assessment)Rent plus appreciation, but lowest liquidity and ongoing holding costs
Tax-sensitive, in a higher bracketDecide on after-tax numbersETF dividends may be taxed separately at 28%; rand interest often falls inside the offshore-income threshold

One closing caveat: this article does not tell you which instrument is better, because that depends on your horizon and your currency needs. When a single number is used to force a decision — "7% beats 5%" — three things have usually been left out: that a distribution can include principal, that tax and fees are deducted, and that the exchange rate moves. South African rand exposure is the third of the three.

FAQ

Is a South African rand deposit better than a Taiwan dividend ETF?

Not on yield alone. An ETF yield divides the distribution by the price and may include equalisation reserve and capital gains; a South African rand deposit rate is a nominal rate quoted by a bank. Decide on your horizon (under one year or over three) and your currency need (TWD or ZAR), then compare after-tax amounts. Section four above runs the same NT$1,000,000 through four layers.

Can an ETF distribution really include my own principal?

Yes. 00878's legal name states that distributions may be paid from the equalisation reserve and that neither income nor distribution is guaranteed. Cathay notes that any part paid from that reserve may reduce the original invested amount. In the February 2025 distribution, 18% was equalisation reserve and 20% capital gains.

Is South African interest taxed at 15% for a non-resident?

The statutory withholding rate on non-resident interest is 15% as a final tax, but section 50D exempts interest paid by a South African bank to a foreign person, so in practice it is usually not withheld. The back-to-back rule in s50D(2) and the days-present rule in s50D(3) still apply, and the bank's current practice governs.

Does rand interest have to be declared in Taiwan?

Offshore income is counted in full only once the household total reaches NT$1,000,000 for the year. On a NT$1,000,000 principal at about 7%, annual interest is roughly NT$70,000, well below the threshold. The basic-income-tax exemption has been NT$7,500,000 since the 2024 tax year, with any excess taxed at 20% before comparison with ordinary income tax.

Should I sell my ETF to fund a South African rand account?

Treat them as different buckets rather than a swap. The ETF is TWD-denominated and settles T+2; the South African rand account involves a remittance cycle of two to four weeks. In most cases it is more sensible to build the rand allocation from new money than to liquidate an existing position.

Will the rand money market rate stay near 7%?

No. the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) raised twice in 2026 — to 7.00% on 28 May and 7.25% on 23 September — with the next decision on 19 November. South African bank rates follow the policy rate, so plan on "about 7%" rather than a single day's best quote.

Why Handle This Through Crestline Advisory?

South African documentation requirements change every year — and what changes is usually the format, not the eligibility. Same passport, same proof of address, wrong format, rejection.

The three most common failure points

  • Passport certification rejected: A plain true-copy stamp is not accepted. A commissioner of oaths must certify in English, confirm the original was seen, add a true-likeness statement for photo pages, and include signature, date, address and occupation.
  • TIN left blank without a reason code: For Taiwanese clients the tax number is the national ID number. Leaving it blank requires ticking Reason A / B / C with an explanation.
  • Proof of address older than three months: Measured from the application date. Past the deadline the entire application is void and must be resubmitted.

Working through our partner Crestline Advisory (on-the-ground execution in South Africa) means these are checked before submission: document format pre-screened item by item (avoiding a 2-4 week round trip), current bank requirements confirmed before you book any flight, remittance routing and BOP declaration categories aligned in advance, and progress tracked locally after submission.
